title: The Good News, the Bad News, and the Start of A Solution for Keeping Distance Learning Simple ance-learning-simple/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Writing in the early weeks of pandemic school closures, Stuart argues that distance learning shares the purpose of in-person teaching, the long-term flourishing of students, and that curriculum coverage is not the point. The good news is that teachers can slow down and be transparent rather than rush to move the whole curriculum online. The bad news is that distance teaching is not the same as classroom teaching and that student motivation, which is highly sensitive to context, has been upended by changes in physical, relational, and emotional space. He warns that pressing on with business as usual risks burnout, disengagement, and resentment for teachers, parents, and students. He then begins offering recommendations for keeping the work simple, centered on enrichment-style activities.
points: The aim of schooling, in person or at a distance, is long-term flourishing, not seamless curriculum delivery.
Skills and lessons that worked in classrooms will only partly transfer to distance teaching.
Motivation depends heavily on context, and the shift to home learning changed that context dramatically.
Pushing to avoid falling behind risks burnout, disengagement, and resentment across the whole system.
Teachers can slow down and keep things simple, favoring enrichment over coverage.
quotes: Education at a distance has as its purpose the same thing as education in person: the promotion of the long-term flourishing of students. In other words, the work of distance learning matters, profoundly, just as the work of in-person learning does.

The point of school isn’t the seamless continuation of the delivery of the curriculum — the point is the long-term flourishing of human beings. To be clear, curricula are super important in seeing that done, but only because as students master the different disciplines laid out in good curricula, they also develop the kinds of knowledge and skills and strengths of character that best predict a flourishing life.
First, education at a distance is not the same thing as education in person. The skills that made us effective classroom teachers won’t transfer neatly into making us effective distance teachers.

In order for a person to learn — whether at a distance or in-person — they’ve got to do work with care. This kind of effortful, careful work is the product of motivation — the Latin root of that word is movere, to move.

So here’s the inescapable thing: human motivation is hugely sensitive to context. The research is clear that you and I have an enormous impact on the motivational contexts that we create in our classrooms.
The psychological, emotional, and spiritual space has changed for all of us. This final shift is profound, and it likely contains our biggest opportunity as educators.

Finally, doing distance education wrong right now may have serious consequences for the long-term flourishing of students, parents/guardians, and teachers. The stakes for doing this wrong are not a few months of lost learning — they are trajectory-shifting burnout for everyone in the system.
